articles/ai1789495200000.title: Why Keeping Customers Matters More Than Winning New Ones
articles/ai1789495200000.teaser: For software companies that sell subscriptions, the real work starts after the contract is signed.
articles/ai1789495200000.text:
When people imagine a successful software company, they often picture a sales team celebrating a big new deal. For companies that sell software as a subscription, however, that moment is only the beginning. The contract might last a year or even just a month, and the customer can walk away at the next renewal date. This is why many subscription businesses now treat customer retention as their most important goal.

The reason is simple economics. Winning a new customer is expensive. Marketing campaigns, sales calls, product demos and free trials all cost money, and it can take many months before a customer has paid enough to cover these costs. If that customer cancels after a short time, the company actually loses money on the deal. On the other hand, a customer who stays for several years becomes more profitable every month, because the cost of serving them is usually much lower than the cost of finding them in the first place.

Experts often describe the problem as a "leaky bucket". Imagine pouring water into a bucket with holes in it. You can pour faster and faster, but if the water keeps running out, the bucket never fills up. In the same way, a company with high churn – the share of customers who cancel – has to keep growing its sales just to stand still. Reducing churn, even slightly, can have a surprisingly large effect on long-term growth.

So how do companies keep their customers? The first step usually happens right after the sale, during onboarding. If new users struggle to set up the product or do not see its value quickly, they are much more likely to leave. That is why many companies offer guided setup, training sessions and simple checklists. Many also build dedicated customer success teams. Unlike traditional support staff, who react to problems, these teams contact customers proactively, check how the product is being used and suggest ways to get more out of it.

Data plays a big role, too. Modern software can show which features customers use and how often they log in. A sudden drop in activity is often an early warning sign that a customer is unhappy or has found an alternative. By spotting these signals early, a company has a chance to fix the problem before the renewal date arrives.

Finally, loyal customers bring benefits that are hard to measure. They are more likely to upgrade to more expensive plans, buy additional features and recommend the product to others. For a small or medium-sized business choosing new software, a recommendation from a satisfied peer is often worth more than any advertisement. In the subscription world, a happy customer is not just revenue – it is also the best marketing a company can have.
keypoints: In subscription software, customers can cancel at every renewal, so retention is a key goal.
Winning new customers is expensive, and a customer only becomes profitable if they stay long enough.
High churn is like a leaky bucket: the company must sell more just to stay at the same size.
Good onboarding, proactive customer success teams and usage data help companies keep customers.
Loyal customers upgrade, buy more and recommend the product, which brings extra growth.

articles/ai1789754400000.title: Your New Colleague Is an Algorithm
articles/ai1789754400000.teaser: AI assistants are arriving in offices everywhere, but using them well is a skill people still need to learn.
articles/ai1789754400000.text:
Only a few years ago, artificial intelligence at work sounded like science fiction. Today, many office workers use AI tools every day, often without thinking much about it. They ask a chatbot to write the first draft of an email, summarise a long report or translate a document. For many people, AI has quietly become a new kind of colleague. But what does this colleague do well, and where does it still need supervision?

The biggest benefit is speed. Tasks that used to take an hour, such as turning meeting notes into a clear summary, can now take a few minutes. AI is especially good at repetitive work with text: sorting incoming documents, pulling key information out of invoices or suggesting answers to common customer questions. This gives employees more time for work that needs human judgement, like building relationships with customers or making difficult decisions.

However, AI tools also make mistakes, and they often make them with great confidence. A chatbot can produce a sentence that sounds perfectly professional but contains wrong facts, invented sources or numbers that do not add up. Experts call this "hallucination". For this reason, many companies tell their staff to treat AI output as a starting point, not a finished product. A human should always check the result before it is sent to a customer or used for an important decision.

There are also questions about data protection. When employees paste confidential information into a public AI tool, they may not know where that data ends up. In Europe, where privacy rules are strict, this is a serious concern. As a result, many organisations now create clear guidelines: which tools are allowed, what kind of information can be shared and who is responsible for the final result. Some companies prefer AI features built directly into the software they already use, so that sensitive data stays in a controlled environment.

Perhaps the most interesting change is in the skills people need. Writing a good instruction for an AI – often called a "prompt" – is a bit like briefing a new intern. You have to explain the context, describe the goal and say what the result should look like. People who can do this clearly tend to get much better results. At the same time, classic skills like critical thinking and good writing become more important, not less, because someone has to judge whether the AI's work is actually good.

In the end, AI is unlikely to replace most office jobs completely, at least not soon. But it is changing them. The workers who benefit most will probably be those who learn to work alongside the technology: using it for the boring parts, checking its work carefully and keeping the important decisions in human hands.

items.excerpt: ViDA represents a fundamental shift in how VAT is administered across the EU.
items.gist: The EU's VAT in the Digital Age package is not another reporting form. It changes who holds the data and when. Member states move from periodic returns to near real-time digital reporting, with transaction data submitted within ten days. The stated driver is the VAT gap, which the Commission puts at roughly 93 billion euros. For a vendor, the interesting part is not the deadline but the leverage: finance teams that have postponed ERP work for years suddenly have a regulatory reason to fund it. The argument that lands in a boardroom is therefore rarely about compliance alone. It is about using a mandate nobody chose as the business case for an integration nobody would otherwise approve.

Notice how rarely a good speaker says a thing is simply better. They say what it is better at, and what they gave up. items.title: The Fed raises rates for the first time since 2023
items.topic_en: US central bank, interest rates and inflation
items.why_de: Zinsentscheidungen tauchen in jeder Wirtschaftsnachricht auf. Wer die Sprache der Notenbanken versteht – hawkish, forward guidance, price stability –, versteht die halbe Finanzpresse.
items.why_en: Rate decisions appear in every piece of economic news. If you understand central-bank language – hawkish, forward guidance, price stability – you understand half of the financial press.
items.excerpt: Inflation is too high and has been for too long.
items.excerptBy: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, quoted via Kiplinger
items.gist: On 16 September the US Federal Reserve raised its key interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent. It was the first increase since 2023, and the vote was unanimous. The reason is simple: the labour market is strong, but inflation has stayed well above the two percent target for years, pushed up partly by high energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. Chair Kevin Warsh refused to say whether more increases will follow. He prefers to look at underlying trends rather than single data points, and he gives markets very little forward guidance. The committee's own projections point to one more hike this year. Markets reacted nervously: long-term bond yields had already climbed to around five percent, their highest level in years.

chunks.note_de: Das Gegenteil ist „to cut rates“. „Increase rates“ geht auch, klingt aber weniger nach Zeitung.

chunks.en: a quarter of a percentage point

chunks.note_de: Das offizielle Ziel jeder Notenbank. Wird oft mit „deliver“ verbunden: „deliver price stability“.

chunks.note_de: Wenn eine Notenbank ankündigt, was sie vorhat. Warsh gibt bewusst wenig davon.
chunks.note_en: When a central bank signals what it plans to do. Warsh deliberately gives little of it.

chunks.note_en: “Well” intensifies here – like “deutlich”. Same with “well below”, “well ahead of”.

items.why_en: The most important relationship in the world economy – and a textbook case of diplomatic language: people say “manage differences” when they mean “conflict”.
items.excerpt: the world's top two economies seek to stabilise a relationship
items.gist: From 23 to 25 September, Chinese President Xi Jinping is on a state visit to the United States – his first to Washington since 2015 and his second meeting with President Trump this year, after Trump travelled to Beijing in May. The timing matters: a one-year trade truce between the two countries is coming to an end. Beijing says both sides want to manage their differences, which covers trade, technology and national security. The programme includes a welcome at the White House, a formal summit and a state dinner that heads of large US technology companies are expected to attend. Xi is travelling with a large business delegation, which shows that the visit is as much about deals as about diplomacy.

items.title: Markets shrug off calls to slow down AI
items.why_de: KI ist das Technologiethema der Jahre – und hier treffen sich drei Sprachwelten: Technik, Ethik und Finanzmarkt. Ideal, um Argumente abzuwägen.
items.why_en: AI is the technology story of these years – and here three kinds of language meet: tech, ethics and finance. Ideal for weighing arguments.
items.excerpt: right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public
items.excerptBy: Sam Altman, quoted by NBC News
items.gist: In mid-September, the heads of two leading AI labs called for the development of more powerful AI models to slow down for safety reasons. One published a long essay over the weekend; the other agreed publicly and said his company would postpone its stock-market listing. Investors reacted at first: chip stocks fell and the Nasdaq dropped by more than one percent in early trading. By the end of the day, however, most of the losses had disappeared, helped by a rally in software and cybersecurity shares. Analysts doubted that the industry would really slow down. Their argument: the race between companies and between countries is so intense that no firm will voluntarily step back while its rivals keep pushing ahead.

lpool/ai1789322400000.title: Why We Sleep Badly
lpool/ai1789322400000.text: Welcome back to Everyday Science. So, today's question comes from a listener who says she's exhausted every morning, even though she's in bed by eleven. And honestly, she's not alone. Researchers who looked at around two thousand adults found that nearly half of them felt tired most days. Now, the usual suspect is the phone, right? Scrolling in bed. And yes, screens do play a part, but interestingly, the study suggests it's not mainly the light. It's the content. If you're reading work emails or arguing with someone online, your brain simply doesn't switch off. Watching a calm nature documentary, on the other hand, seems to do very little harm. The other big factor was irregular timing. People who went to bed at wildly different times at the weekend slept worse during the week, almost like a mini jet lag. So what's the advice? Well, keep your bedtime roughly the same, even on Saturdays, and if you really can't leave the phone alone, at least avoid anything stressful in the last hour. Small changes, but they seem to add up.

lpool/ai1789668000000.title: Onboarding a New Customer
lpool/ai1789668000000.text: Right, quick briefing on Fairfield Logistics before tomorrow's kick-off call. They're a mid-sized company, about a hundred and forty employees, and they've been storing everything on an old file server plus, well, a lot of paper. They've signed up for our cloud plan, starting with the finance and HR departments. Now, a couple of things to watch out for. First, their IT manager, Tom, is quite sceptical. He wasn't the one who chose us, the managing director was, so expect a lot of questions about data security and where the servers are located. Make sure you mention that everything's hosted in Frankfurt. Second, they want the HR files migrated first, which is the more sensitive data, so we'll need to agree access rights before we move a single document. My suggestion is that we don't overload them. Let's aim for a pilot with around twenty users in the first month, get some quick wins, and only then roll it out to the whole finance team. Any questions before we wrap up?

writing/w1789408800000.title: Explaining a delivery delay
writing/w1789408800000.task: Write a semi-formal email to an existing customer explaining that the new mobile scanning feature they were promised will be released three weeks later than planned. Apologise, give the reason in simple terms and say what happens next.
writing/w1789408800000.text: Dear Mr Walker, unfortunately the delivery of the scanners is delayed by two weeks, because our supplier has problems with the chips. We are very sorry for this. We propose to start the training earlier so that your team is ready when the devices arrive.
